title: Dual Constraints of Microbial Carbon Use Efficiency and Mineral Protection Govern Necromass Accrual
content:
Microbial necromass is an important contributor to organic carbon accumulation in soil, but its response to fertilization varies with environmental conditions. Across 14 long-term fertilization experiments in China, manure application promoted necromass accumulation most strongly under resource-limited conditions, where microbial production was the main constraint; under resource-abundant conditions, mineral preservation became dominant. This context dependence has important implications for soil carbon management and responses to global change.


ABSTRACT

Increasing soil organic carbon (SOC), central to food security and climate mitigation, is increasingly recognized as being mediated by microbial necromass C (MNC) accrual. However, how microbial production and mineral preservation jointly govern MNC accrual under contrasting resource conditions remains unclear. Here, we analyzed soils from 14 long-term fertilization experiments (up to 47 years) to assess how edaphic and climatic conditions regulate the response of MNC accrual to manure (M) and non-manure (NM) fertilization treatments. We found that the primary constraints on MNC accrual varied with resource availability, with microbial production under resource-limited conditions and mineral preservation under resource-abundant conditions. Under resource-limited conditions, M treatments increased MNC by up to 122%, with changes tightly coupled to SOC gains. This accrual was associated with increases in dissolved organic C and microbial C use efficiency, indicating a production-constrained pathway in which manure inputs alleviate substrate limitation and promote microbial C allocation toward biomass production and necromass formation. Conversely, under resource-abundant conditions, MNC responses to fertilization were weaker (+56%) and uncoupled from SOC gains. Instead, MNC accrual was primarily associated with mineral protection capacity (e.g., Fe and Al oxides), consistent with a preservation-constrained pathway. Overall, microbial processing and mineral preservation represent context-dependent constraints on MNC accrual under contrasting resource conditions. These findings underscore the importance of resource context for site-specific C management and for understanding soil C dynamics under global change.
